title: Polynomial Separation between One-Way and Two-Way LOCC in Discrimination of Maximally Entangled States
abstract: One-way local operations and classical communication (LOCC) can fail to distinguish four orthogonal maximally entangled states in every local dimension $d\ge4$. We show that every set of $k$ pairwise orthogonal maximally entangled states in $\mathbb C^d\otimes\mathbb C^d$ is perfectly distinguishable by an $A\to B\to A$ protocol whenever $d\ge Ck^4[\log(2k)]^ν$, for universal constants $C,ν>0$. A single feedback message therefore raises the number of candidates that can always be distinguished from a constant to $Ω\!\left(d^{1/4}/(\log d)^{ν/4}\right)$, establishing a polynomial separation between one-way and two-way LOCC. In our protocol, Alice preserves exact orthogonality while reducing overlaps between Bob's conditional subspaces. Bob reduces the candidates to a singleton or an orthogonal pair and refines his outcome so that Alice can complete the discrimination. As a corollary, nine copies suffice for perfect two-way LOCC discrimination of any orthogonal maximally entangled set in all sufficiently large local dimensions.
summary: This paper rigorously proves a polynomial separation between the distinguishability of orthogonal maximally entangled states using one-way versus two-way LOCC. By designing a feedback protocol ($A 	o B 	o A$), the authors show that two-way communication allows distinguishing exponentially more states than one-way communication. This establishes a key resource advantage of classical feedback in quantum information processing.
main_problem: The paper establishes a quantitative separation between the distinguishability of orthogonal maximally entangled states (MESs) using one-way versus two-way Local Operations and Classical Communication (LOCC).
main_result: Two-way LOCC allows for the perfect discrimination of a set size that grows polynomially with the local dimension $d$, contrasting sharply with the constant bound achievable with one-way LOCC.
method: The authors develop protocols involving sequential quantum measurements and classical feedback ($A 	o B 	o A$) to bound the number of distinguishable states, relying on advanced techniques from quantum information theory.
model_or_system: The system under study consists of sets of orthogonal maximally entangled states in the tensor product space $\mathbb{C}^d \otimes \mathbb{C}^d$. The analysis compares the limitations imposed by one-way versus two-way communication channels.
key_observables: The number of pairwise orthogonal MESs ($k$) that can be perfectly distinguished, quantified by $m_{	o}(d)$ and $m_{\leftrightarrow}(d)$.
important_parameters: Local dimension $d$, the number of states $k$, and the communication structure (one-way vs. two-way LOCC).
main_assumptions: The results concern the perfect distinguishability of *every* set of orthogonal MESs, and the analysis provides sufficient conditions and necessary lower bounds.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the two-way discrimination protocol for $k=4$, detailing the sequence of quantum systems and classical messages ($A 	o B 	o A$). Table I summarizes the worst-case thresholds for different communication classes.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the limitations of one-way LOCC (constant distinguishability) and then constructing a protocol using two-way LOCC that achieves a polynomial lower bound on the distinguishable set size, culminating in a universal copy bound.
why_interesting: The quantitative separation between one-way and two-way communication protocols in quantum state discrimination is a fundamental result in quantum communication theory, providing concrete bounds on the power of classical feedback.
